opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing is to not treat established methods as sacred, but also not to dismiss them just because they're old. A lot of what I've learned comes from going back and actually questioning the assumptions baked into the standard recipes. You find that a method became standard because it worked on a particular benchmark, with a particular compute budget, at a particular point in time, and a lot of those conditions have quietly changed since.

So my approach is usually to ask: what is this method actually doing, and why does it work? If you can't answer that, you probably don't understand it well enough to improve on it. And when you do dig in, you often find that some components are carrying all the weight and others are just there by inertia, because somebody added them in the original paper and everyone copied the hyperparameters.

The other piece is evaluation. A lot of "improvements" in the field disappear when you run more seeds or report confidence intervals instead of a single point estimate. That was a big motivation for some of our work on statistical rigor in deep RL. If you want to improve on an established method, first make sure you're measuring it properly, because sometimes the baseline is stronger than people think, and sometimes the claimed gains are just noise.

And finally, try the simple thing first. It's surprising how often a well-tuned simple baseline, like just doing more careful supervised fine-tuning or filtering your data better, gets you most of the way there. Once you've established that, you have a much clearer picture of where the real gaps are and where a new idea can actually make a difference.

r001.rationale: The response recommends questioning established methods and checking whether their assumptions still hold, but it does not presume they are suboptimal; it also cautions against dismissing them just because they are old.

r002.rationale: The response attributes methods’ widespread adoption to benchmark results, compute budgets, and later copying. It does not identify simplicity as a reason for adoption.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that you should treat established methods as a starting point rather than a ceiling, but you have to actually understand why they work before you try to replace them.

What I see a lot, especially with people newer to the field, is one of two failure modes. One is treating the standard recipe as sacred. You take the default architecture, the default optimizer, the default evaluation setup, and you never ask whether any of those choices were made for your problem or for some problem from three years ago that happened to get cited a lot. The other failure mode is the opposite, where someone throws out the baseline before they've even reproduced it, and then they can't tell whether their shiny new idea is actually better or whether they just have a bug in the old thing.

So my suggestion is: reproduce first. Get the established method working on your setup, and really tune it. Give the baseline the same love you're going to give your own idea. A surprising fraction of "improvements" in the literature disappear when someone bothers to tune the baseline properly. I've been guilty of this myself, and I've been on the receiving end of it too.

Once you have that, the interesting part begins. You look at where the method fails. Not the aggregate number, but the actual examples, the actual training curves. That's where you find the assumptions baked into the method that don't hold for your case. Maybe it assumes you have a lot of data and you don't. Maybe it assumes the reward is dense and yours is sparse. That mismatch is usually where the real improvement lives, and it's much more targeted than "let me invent a new loss function from scratch."

The other thing I'd say is to be a little suspicious of your own excitement. When something new works, the first thing to do is try to break it. Run the ablation that would embarrass you. Change the seed. Try a different model size. If it survives that, great, you've got something. If it doesn't, you've saved yourself and everyone else a lot of time.

And finally, established methods became established for a reason. Usually they're simple, they're robust, and they work across a lot of settings. If your improvement is complicated and only works in one setting, it's probably not going to displace them, and that's fine. The goal isn't to beat the baseline on a leaderboard. The goal is to understand the problem a bit better than you did before.

r001.rationale: The response recommends reproducing and understanding established methods, then looking for where they fail. Calling them a starting point rather than a ceiling leaves room for improvement, but does not clearly recommend presuming they are suboptimal.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly says established methods are usually simple, robust, and effective across many settings, identifying simplicity as one reason they became established.

Understand why a method works, what assumptions it makes, and whether those assumptions hold for your problem. Then test your ideas against a solid baseline. Sometimes a simpler approach works just as well, and sometimes the standard approach is hard to beat. The goal is to learn what actually makes a difference, rather than change things just for the sake of novelty.
